items.content:
New lecture on pwncollege, presented by guest lecturer Jennifer Miller (Zolutal) from the SEPCOM lab, provides an introduction to Linux kernel security and exploitation concepts within the context of the CSE466 course (0:00-0:15).

Key takeaways from the lecture:

> Kernel Basics: The kernel acts as the interface between hardware and userland applications, handling task scheduling and interprocess communication (1:08-1:36).

> Kernel Modules: These are extensions to the kernel, ranging from drivers to security modules. They can be in-tree (part of the kernel source) or out-of-tree (proprietary/external) (2:46-3:51).
Interacting with Modules: The lecture demonstrates how modules expose functionality to user space, specifically through `/proc` entries and the `ioctl` system call (3:51-6:07).

Exploitation Concepts:
> Privilege Escalation: A primary goal, often involving the manipulation of the `task_struct` and `cred` structures to set the effective UID to 0 (root) (11:03-13:09).

> Memory Protections: Discusses mitigations like KASLR (Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization), which randomizes memory positions (15:08-16:00).

> Kernel Shellcoding: Unlike user space, kernel shellcode calls internal kernel functions directly. The lecture demonstrates allocating RWX (Read-Write-Execute) memory pages and triggering execution through a modified kernel module (8:51-11:03, 42:00-58:50).

> Debugging: The lecture provides practical guidance on using GDB to interact with the guest kernel, noting the challenges of debugging with hardware-assisted virtualization and the benefits of using emulator mode (7:55-8:41, 51:42-55:17).

طبق پروتکل‌های ضدجاسوسی واشنگتن، خاک چین منطقه‌ای آلوده از نظر سایبری به حساب می‌آید و هیچ مقام آمریکایی اجازه ندارد گوشی شخصی، لپ‌تاپ یا حتی کابل شارژش را از هواپیما بیرون ببرد. به همه‌ی اعضای هیئت گوشی یک‌بارمصرف می‌دهند و موقع برگشت، همه‌ی دستگاه‌ها و کارت‌های تردد را پیش از ورود به کابین جمع می‌کنند و از بین می‌برند. این حساسیت در پایان نشست ۱۹ نوامبر شنژن به جایی رسید که حتی گوشی خبرنگاران همراه ترامپ هم پای پله‌های هواپیما ضبط شد تا هیچ وسیله‌ای که به دکل یا وای‌فای چین وصل شده، به آمریکا برنگردد (گزارش هیئت رسانه‌ای کاخ سفید در پایان سفر شنژن).

اما ماجرا فقط به گوشی‌ها محدود نمی‌شود؛ ترامپ هیچ غذا یا نوشیدنی‌ای را که میزبان آماده کرده باشد، نمی‌خورد و نمی‌نوشد. نگرانی سرویس مخفی فقط سم نیست؛ ردیاب‌های نانویی و برداشتن نمونه‌ی دی‌ان‌ای از لیوان و ظرف‌ها برای ساختن پرونده‌ی ژنتیکی و پزشکی او هم مطرح است. گفت‌وگوهای حساس را در اتاقک‌های سیارِ ضدشنود انجام می‌دهند و بعد از فرود در آمریکا، همه‌ی اعضای هیئت دوباره بررسی‌های کامل ضدجاسوسی را می‌گذرانند تا هیچ اثری از نفوذ ۴۸ ساعته باقی نماند (پروتکل‌های حفاظتی و ضدجاسوسی سفرهای پرخطر آمریکا).

نقطه‌ی کور ماجرا همین‌جاست: همان فناوریِ تفتیش عمیق اینترنت، شنود مخابراتی و آلوده‌کردن سخت‌افزار که واشنگتن را وادار می‌کند گوشی‌هایش را فیزیکی نابود کند، همان زیرساختی است که پکن سال‌هاست به تهران می‌فروشد و حالا پشت سیم‌کارت‌ها، اپ‌های داخلی و فیلترشکن‌های رایگان قرار دارد.

وقتی سرویس مخفی آمریکا به وای‌فای و حتی لیوان آب پکن اعتماد ندارد، یعنی در یک شبکه‌ی آلوده هیچ سپر نرم‌افزاری ارزانی وجود ندارد. فرقِ در امان ماندن و آسیب‌دیدن فقط به این بستگی دارد که این واقعیت را قبل از دیر شدن بفهمی یا بعدش.

items.content:
I think there’s a major misunderstanding in this discussion.

The growing number of vulnerabilities discovered in open source software doesn’t necessarily mean that open source code is worse than proprietary software.

What we’re seeing is a massive increase in scrutiny.

For years, many open source projects simply didn’t receive thorough security reviews. Nobody had the time, resources or financial incentive to look that closely.

Now anyone with access to a capable LLM can point it at a public repository and start looking for vulnerabilities. And newer models are getting remarkably good at finding issues that previous tools and human reviewers missed.

But something very similar is happening behind closed doors.

I can tell you from our own experience, and from discussions with people at other software companies, that internal development teams are also struggling with a flood of findings from AI-assisted code reviews.

Many of these findings concern code that has been running in production for years. In proprietary software development, they rarely become public CVEs or security advisories. They end up as Jira tickets, creating backlogs that take weeks or months to process.

Ironically, while AI accelerates software development, it’s also slowing teams down by exposing years of accumulated technical debt and security issues that nobody had identified before.

So I’d be careful about interpreting the current wave of open source vulnerabilities as evidence of lower code quality.

items.content:
when you are operating on a red team, think of the potential consequence of every single action. not taking action is generally good. there are ops when time is a factor, but in most cases, i think its good to simply pause, wait, think. 

you should think about the possible consequence of any action, no matter how 'small'. every action after successful initial infection, is likely logged, somewhere. every single thing you do, is inevitably 'seen' at some level. the difference in your success is whether or not it is bubbled up to a human or automated security product with response capability.

now of course, you can get a sense of some small actions that are consistently 'safe'. but i would caution against trusting your mental list so quickly. it is easy to become complacent, to think 'this is always safe' without really considering all the variables or unknowns, of your current environment. take pause. reassess. 

the idea should be to take the time and spend the mental effort, to imagine the possible downsides, visibility, artifacts, any possible IOCs that will be generated. build a confidence level for that next considered action. reassess if you have other options to achieve the same effect. in fact, do you even need this piece of data or escalation? perhaps not? is there a safer way to reach the same goal? these are the questions to ask yourself before you make the next move.

items.content:
MIT researchers found a CPU side-channel called Interrupt Injection that cuts straight through Spectre v2 defenses on both AMD and Intel chips.

By arranging a hardware interrupt to arrive precisely at the right moment, unprivileged user-space code can re-poison the branch predictor after the defense has executed but before the CPU relies on the prediction. 

The timing window exists in the gap between OS implementation and CPU protection. You can pull Linux password hashes from kernel memory despite modern mitigations.
